plan.chapterName: OpenStax Precalculus 2e, chapter 8: Further Applications of Trigonometry
plan.contextChunk: This figure sets four triangle sketches in a row, labeled (a) through (d) below, to enumerate the possible outcomes when two sides and a non-included angle are known. All four share one labeling scheme: an acute angle alpha marked by an arc at the left end of a horizontal base, a vertex beta at the right end of that base, an apex gamma above, side b rising from alpha to gamma, and side a hanging from gamma. Panel (a), headed No triangle, a < h, draws a as a short vertical segment from gamma that stops above the base, leaving a visible gap so nothing closes. Panel (b), headed Right triangle, a = h, has a reaching the base exactly at beta, with a small square marking the right angle formed there. Panel (c), headed Two triangles, a > h, a < b, shows a solid vertical altitude labeled h from gamma to the base, plus two dashed segments each labeled a running from gamma to different landing points, one to the left of the altitude's foot and one at beta. Panel (d), headed One triangle, a is greater than or equal to b, shows a broad triangle whose side a slopes from gamma down to beta. Aligning the four under identical labels isolates the one quantity that changes, the length of a measured against the altitude and against b, and shows how many closures each case admits.

interactionPlan.concept: When two sides and a non-included angle (SSA) are given, comparing side a to the altitude h = b·sin(α) and to side b determines whether zero, one (right), two, or one triangle can be constructed.
elements: four side-by-side panels labeled (a), (b), (c), (d) with headings: 'No triangle, a < h', 'Right triangle, a = h', 'Two triangles, a > h, a < b', 'One triangle, a ≥ b'
horizontal base line in each panel with angle α marked by an arc at the left end and vertex β labeled at the right end
side b drawn as a fixed segment rising from α to apex γ, labeled 'b'
apex labeled γ in each panel
panel (a): short vertical segment labeled 'a' hanging from γ, stopping above the base with a visible gap
panel (b): vertical side 'a' from γ reaching the base exactly at β, with a small right-angle square at β
panel (c): solid vertical altitude from γ to the base labeled 'h', plus two dashed segments each labeled 'a' from γ to the base — one landing left of the altitude foot, one landing at β
panel (d): side 'a' drawn as a solid slanted segment from γ down to β, completing a broad triangle
interactive construction view: fixed α and b, candidate side a swinging from γ like a compass arc toward the base, with altitude h guide line

interactions.label: Side length a (α and b fixed)
interactions.teaches: The number of possible triangles is not arbitrary — it is decided entirely by comparing a to h and to b: below h nothing closes, at h exactly one right triangle, between h and b two triangles, at or above b exactly one

interactions.label: Show altitude h
interactions.teaches: The altitude h = b·sin(α) is the critical threshold: it is the shortest distance from γ to the base, which is why a < h can never reach the base and a = h reaches it at exactly one perpendicular point

interactions.label: Step through cases
interactions.teaches: Each inequality for a corresponds to one distinct geometric outcome — stepping through them in order shows the progression as a grows from 'too short to close' to 'long enough to swing past b'

demo_steps.title: No triangle: a < h
demo_steps.narration: Side a is shorter than the altitude h, the shortest possible distance from γ to the base — the segment dangles with a visible gap and no triangle can close.

demo_steps.title: Right triangle: a = h
demo_steps.narration: When a exactly equals h, it just reaches the base at one perpendicular point — the right-angle marker appears and exactly one (right) triangle exists.

demo_steps.title: Two triangles: h < a < b
demo_steps.narration: Now a is longer than h but shorter than b, so it can swing to the base on either side of the altitude foot — the two dashed positions both close, giving two valid triangles.

demo_steps.title: One triangle: a ≥ b
demo_steps.narration: Once a is at least as long as b, the left-hand landing point falls behind α and is no longer valid — only one triangle remains.

demo_steps.title: Explore freely
demo_steps.narration: Drag the slider for a slowly and watch the construction pass through all four regimes; toggle the altitude off and on to confirm h is the boundary that separates 'impossible' from 'possible'.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The ambiguous case of SSA is fully resolved by two comparisons: a against h = b·sin(α) decides whether any triangle exists, and a against b decides whether one or two exist.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate the four-panel static figure faithfully — identical labeling scheme across panels (α with arc at left of horizontal base, β at right, γ apex, b from α to γ, a from γ), panel headings exactly as in the original, panel (a) showing the dangling a with visible gap, panel (b) with the right-angle square at β, panel (c) with solid altitude h and two dashed a segments, panel (d) as a broad closed triangle. Alongside (or as the main interactive view), build a single live construction: fixed α (about 35–40°) and fixed b, with side a pivoting from γ whose length is set by the slider; draw a faint arc showing where the tip of a can land on the base. When altitude is shown, draw the dashed vertical h with right-angle marker at its foot. Highlight the active case's closing side(s) or gap as the stepper advances, and show the current inequality (e.g. 'h < a < b → two triangles') as a caption. Use one consistent color for fixed elements (black/dark) and an accent color (e.g. blue for a, red for h) so the changing quantity stands out.

authoredContext:
Oblique triangles in the category SSA may have four different outcomes. The figure illustrates the solutions with the known sides a and b and known angle α.

Four attempted oblique triangles are in a row, all with standard labels. Side c is the horizontal base. In the first attempted triangle, side a is less than the altitude height. Since side a cannot reach side c, there is no triangle. In the second attempted triangle, side a is equal to the length of the altitude height, so side a forms a right angle with side c. In the third attempted triangle, side a is greater than the altitude height and less than side b, so side a can form either an acute or obtuse angle with side c. In the fourth attempted triangle, side a is greater than or equal to side b, so side a forms an acute angle with side c.

evaluation.notes: All four SSA panels (no triangle / right / two / one triangle) are reproduced with correct topology, labels, and the h and dashed-a conventions, and the added slider-driven construction with step player and altitude toggle genuinely teaches the a-vs-h-vs-b comparison; the main flaws are the α=40° vs 36.9° inconsistency between the two halves and the cramped small panels.

Fix the case stepper to start at case 0 on the first click (initialize caseIdx = -1) instead of skipping directly to 'Right triangle'.
Drop or restyle the 'gap' label/dashed connector in the a < h live case so it reads as an annotation rather than a new geometric element.
